Post title: The Future Without the Dead

Imagine waking up on a world that looks remarkably the same as today plus the timestamp tells us the year 1999. In our timeline, Aukland staff are still desk-bound by late 1999, and the internet has developed slowly. But what if we sorted it differently? How would our present feel if history'd been sorted differently?

The fundamental issue is population density. By 1999 standards, the number and proportions of elderly people globally skew heavily toward wealthy urban centers. Japan, the UK, Canada—everyone over 55 has become bankers, lawyers, investors, or doctors. They travel fast, vote, and accumulate wealth. In Aukland, that means certain demographic clusters would also decay faster. A thirty-year-old settlement couldn't wipe out itself without revision.

That doesn't mean avoiding aging entirely. It means we'll need to walk differently. Cities where older generations retire first often become regional knowledge hubs instead of gated communities. Using parks and community centres the way NZ did during the 90s, rather than keeping everyone locked in tenancy. The irony is useful—we'd see tradition flourish alongside new infrastructure. Heck, barbeque clubs existed thirty years ago, long after retirement actually started flourishing.

There's also humor to include. My old jokes about old people complaining they're too young to do the same things
